items.log_text: Fine basement clay thinned with water to slip consistency. Wood ash added as flux — unwashed, still alkaline. Iron scale from the corroded shelving stirred in for colour. Test tile painted and fired. The glaze melted partially: a semi-matte surface, brown-black with a slight sheen. Usable.

Washed wood ash reduces the alkalinity spike. Yellow ochre from the oxidised rubble — scrubbed and dried. Applied over a bisque bowl. Fired at eight-forty. The glaze ran slightly at the base: ochre-tan, semi-transparent. Where it pooled, a richer amber. Pleasant.

Manganese ore found in the old electrical panel fittings — crushed and powdered through doubled cloth. Added to the ash-flux slip. Test tile fired dark brown to near-black. Surface is matte and dense. No runny areas. This could be a reliable glaze if we can source more manganese.

Bone ash as an alternative flux — fired and powdered vertebrae. Creates a softer, milkier melt than wood ash. Combined with iron scale the surface came out a muted grey-green on this test tile. Less predictable than the wood ash batches; more interesting.

Mortar scraping slip without colorant — testing the base flux alone. The tile fired white-cream. Clean and opaque. Not exciting but it is the most archivally useful: a neutral glaze for vessels meant to hold food. No metallic contamination.

Stripped copper from salvage wire and filed it to fine dust. Mixed into the washed ash slip at low percentage. Test tile fired green — unexpected richness. The copper oxide colouration is strong even at two percent addition. The colour variation across the tile suggests reduction at the surface.

Mixed base clay — less predictable. Some areas of the test tile showed the glaze blistering where the rubble clay's coarser particles sat under the slip. Iron-scale colour was there but uneven. Acceptable for storage vessels. Not for anything that needs to hold liquid cleanly.
